segments.title: Why historians do not cite Wikipedia
segments.body: A citation should let another reader return to the same evidence and identify the person or work responsible for it. A Wikipedia entry has no single author who can be held accountable for an error. Its editable nature usually helps keep pages current, but it also allows bad actors to alter them. Because the text can change after consultation, the page does not remain a fixed reference. Historical research depends on other scholars being able to retrace the evidence and reach a comparable result.

evidence.note: Wikipedia lacks a single accountable author and can change after consultation, making it an unstable citation.

segments.summary: Historians use Wikipedia, but its text can change and no single author is accountable for it. Those qualities make it unsuitable as a stable citation.
segments.question: Why do historians avoid citing Wikipedia even though they use it?
segments.answerShort: A Wikipedia page has no single accountable author and can change after a researcher reads it, so another scholar may not be able to consult the same text.

segments.title: Wikipedia as a research starting point
segments.body: Wikipedia can help begin research on an unfamiliar subject. The references at the bottom of an entry provide an initial source list. Those works lead to their own bibliographies and sources, allowing the research to expand beyond the page. Wikipedia is a signpost toward citable material rather than the authority supporting the final claim. The site is also useful for finding images for explanatory videos.

evidence.note: Wikipedia can begin research by pointing readers toward sources, further bibliographies, and usable images.

segments.summary: On an unfamiliar subject, historians can use Wikipedia to find cited works and then follow those works' own bibliographies and sources.

segments.title: Citation styles and the flow of an argument
segments.body: Harvard places citations in parentheses within the text, while Chicago uses footnotes and Vancouver uses endnotes. All three systems serve the same basic purpose, but each places the reference differently. Historians often prefer notes because repeated brackets can interrupt the flow of an analytical argument and make the case less persuasive. Footnotes keep the source close to the passage for readers who want to check it. Publishers often prefer endnotes because they are easier to place in print, so the choice also reflects production needs.

evidence.note: Harvard places citations in the text, Chicago uses footnotes, and Vancouver uses endnotes, each affecting an argument's visual flow differently.

segments.summary: Harvard, Chicago, and Vancouver all identify sources, but footnotes and endnotes interfere less with the flow of historical prose than repeated parenthetical citations.
segments.question: Why do historians often prefer Chicago or Vancouver citation styles?
segments.answerShort: Their footnotes or endnotes preserve the flow of an argument while still allowing readers to trace its sources.
